Grammy-winning musician Silvana Estrada to program Latin music at the LA Phil
Adolfo Guzman-Lopez
is an arts and general assignment reporter on LAist's Explore LA team.
Published November 21, 2026 at 5:00 AM PST
Silvana Estrada, the Grammy-winning musician who has been named the Creative Chair of Latin Music at the LA Phil.
Courtesy LA Phil)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
Listen
3:39
Silvana Estrada: Rising star, Grammy winner and LA Phil's new creative chair for Latin Music
Adolfo Guzman-Lopez has this profile.
There was a moment of uncertainty after the host at this year’s Latin Grammys read Silvana Estrada’s name as the winner of the award for Best Singer-Songwriter Song.
The TV camera couldn’t find her. Then, from the rear of the hall, running out of the darkness, wavy hair tossing from side to side, Estrada appeared.
“I was like, ’Oh my God, what is this? This is a dream,’” Estrada told LAist.
Silvana Estrada performs at the Ford Amphitheater in L.A. with members of Youth Orchestra Los Angeles.
Courtesy LA Phil )
“My team and I, we've been working so, so, so hard this year and for the last 10 years we've been really … building this beautiful project,” she said.
That beautiful project is centered around her melodic voice, solid musicianship and poetic songwriting that explores the shades of love and loss.
About a week before the Latin Grammys, she'd also been recognized by the Los Angeles Philharmonic, which appointed her to a post it had just created creative chair for Latin music.
Sponsored message
“It's such a dream. … I feel just absolutely honored, and I want to do my best. Every day I'm writing in my notes all sorts of ideas, who I want to bring, how I want to do it,” she said.
Sanctuary for Latin culture
The appointment of the Mexico-based singer-songwriter comes on the heels of years of creative work in the U.S. She first gained public attention in 2022, when she won Best New Artist at the Latin Grammys for her album Marchita. That was followed by several high-profile appearances, including NPR’s Tiny Desk and Jimmy Kimmel Live! with members of the LA Phil.
Silvana Estrada performing at Disney Hall
Courtesy LA Phil )
Her new role stands to establish Estrada as a cultural tastemaker in Southern California as she programs several concerts next year. It's a door opened after LA Phil music director Gustavo Dudamel, who was born and raised in Venezuela, invited her to perform in L.A. over the years. Dudamel left the LA Phil in August to become music director of the New York Philharmonic.
“The LA Phil is that sort of sanctuary for the Latino culture and many, many communities who find a … space to be seen,” Estrada said.
"This is big"
The appointment of a Mexican singer-songwriter by such an established L.A. cultural institution is not going unnoticed.
Sponsored message
“It's great to see that an organization like LA Phil is thinking outside the box,” said Pilar Diaz, a longtime music educator in L.A. schools and the lead singer of the L.A. rock band Los Abandoned.
It's great to see that an organization like LA Phil is thinking outside the box.
— Pilar Diaz, L.A. music educator
Diaz, who was born in Chile but grew up in the San Fernando Valley, credits Dudamel’s 17-year tenure with opening the doors to make Estrada’s appointment happen.
“This feels like … for me as an Angeleno and as a Chilena woman and a musician … this is big,” she said.
Selecting Estrada, she said, feels like what happens in Chile, where cultural organizations are more inclined to tap artists to curate and program events.
Estrada was born and raised in Veracruz, Mexico. The state capital, a port city with a long musical tradition that blends Indigenous, African and European sounds, is not unlike that of New Orleans. Some people with ties to both Mexico and Veracruz hail the appointment.
“We feel pride, we feel proud of Latinos in general … so now imagine being Mexican, and then being from Veracruz,” said Cesar Castro, who’s from Veracruz and teaches son jarocho, a regional style, at UCLA and Occidental College.
Sponsored message
He admires Estrada, he said, for being firmly rooted in her home region and country, but he’s expecting the shows she programs to look beyond.
“I don't appreciate the Mexican centrism that some people have. So it would be a good chance to have that platform to represent other regions of the continent of Latino culture,” he said, like music from Central America and Peru.
Next season's performances
Estrada is set to program three performances in the 2027-2028 season, she said, choosing from among the LA Phil’s three venues — Disney Hall, the Hollywood Bowl and the Ford Amphitheater. One of the shows will include her in performance. For now, she’s not naming specific performers she plans to invite. Whoever it is, she said, she wants Southern California audiences to see the richness of what Latin American performing arts have to offer, the United States included.
“It's very important to especially embrace the richness of our culture and the dialogue between our culture with other cultures and also between our countries,” she said.
It's very important to especially embrace the dialogue between our culture with other cultures and also between our countries.
— Silvana Estrada
Estrada has performed throughout the U.S. and Latin America in recent years. Her 2025 album, Vendrán Suaves Lluvias (Soft Rains Will Come) is centered around the death and feeling of loss of her best friend four years ago.

Born after the Eaton Fire, Backyard Party opens a permanent music venue for teens in Pasadena
Josie Huang
is a reporter and Weekend Edition host who spotlights the people and places at the heart of our region.
Published November 21, 2026 at 5:00 AM PST
The rock punk outfit Squatchy played to a crowd of teens from all over L.A. during the opening of Backyard Party's permanent venue in Pasadena.
Josie Huang
LAist)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
Listen
4:01
Kids displaced by the Eaton Fire now has a permanent place to play and see gigs
Backyard Party has a forever home. Josie Huang reports.
Inside a cavernous warehouse in northwest Pasadena, teenagers skanked to the punk band Squatchy, hair flying and arms flailing beneath a wash of purple light.
It was opening night for Backyard Party’s new permanent home, a milestone for the music nonprofit that’s spent the past year bouncing from venue to venue, staging shows for young bands.
The project formed after the Eaton Fire destroyed many of the backyards, garages and schools where young musicians might otherwise have performed.
If you go: Backyard Party
What: All-ages, alcohol-free live music shows featuring young bands, plus creative workshops and other events.
When: Regular Saturday shows, with additional events on select dates. Check the calendar for times.
Where: 1250 Lincoln Ave., Pasadena, CA 91103
Tickets: Typically $10–$15
More information at the Backyard Party website.
Since then, Backyard Party has held dozens of pop-ups at shops, homes and other borrowed spaces.
The new Backyard Party venue sits in a business park off of the 210 Freeway, near Pasadena's border with Altadena.
Josie Huang
LAist)
In a full-circle turn, it's landed in the same business park off of the 210 where its first show took place in September 2025, just a few doors away from a space half the size of the new location.
Sponsored message
"It'll be really nice to have a spot that everyone knows to go to, and they're like, 'Oh, that's the spot," said 16-year-old Layne Brisbois who came from Glendale.
A homecoming
During last Saturday’s opening night, teen volunteers who help run the show and oversee the merch table also took on the task of decorating the new space, plastering the walls with drawings from floor to ceiling.
Putting down stakes in Pasadena had always been the plan, but affordable spaces were hard to find.
Backyard Park was on the verge of moving to a space in Cypress Park, the reasoning being that a more central location would be easier for bands and fans traveling from all over Southern California to play Backyard Party.
In the span of a night, volunteers, bands and fans had covered the walls of the new venue with art and sayings.
Josie Huang
LAist)
"We had no idea that there were literally hundreds of teenage bands,” said co-founder Sandra Denver, whose own teenage daughter plays in a band. "It's way bigger than we thought it was going to be.”
Sponsored message
But then the Cypress Park deal fell through just days before that venue was supposed to officially open.
With little time to spare, fellow co-founder Matt Chait reached out to the Pasadena business park landlord, who happened to have a 2,600-square-foot location available.
The turnout on opening night helped reaffirm their decision to secure the space.
"When the tickets rolled in, I saw the pre-sales, and I was seeing like Chino and Fresno," Chait said. "I'm like, ‘Holy cow!’ These people are driving out here for a $12 show. That's kind of amazing."
Backyard Party co-founder Sandra Denver looks on as the new venue in Pasadena marked its opening night.
Josie Huang
LAist)
Backyard Party co-founder Matt Chait engineers the sound at the opening of the new venue.
Josie Huang
LAist)
Keeping tickets affordable — generally $10 to $15 — is a priority for Backyard Party, as is paying every band that performs. To help cover expenses, the nonprofit relies on donations, sponsorships and partnerships.
A place to connect
Backyard Party joins a small club of alcohol-free spaces catering to teens, like The Smell in downtown and The Haven in Pomona.
Sponsored message
In the last year, friendships forged at Backyard Party shows have taken on a life of their own, bringing young musicians together who’ve gone on to form bands.
A group of teenage friends relax in the parking lot outside Backyard Party in between acts. (From left to right: Layne Brisbois, Maui Ruiz, Kovas Radevenis, Alexis Reyes and
Jett Bizon.)
Josie Huang
LAist)
And it’s given teens like 17-year-old Maui Ruiz, who came from Whittier, a place to express themselves and be taken seriously.
"Adults see us as if we know nothing at all," he said. "But if you really take some time and sit down with, like, a 17-year-old, 16-year-old, they know a lot more than you think. It is important for us to have place to just sing about it."
Sitting in the parking lot with musician friends between acts, Ruiz imagined returning to Backyard Party years from now and remembering what happened here.
"Every time people pass it’s, like, ‘Oh my God, that's history,’” he said. "This is about to become history, and we need a place like that."
While Backyard Party is geared toward teens, some younger fans are already getting in on the action.
Sponsored message
Pearl McClenaghan, 14, came with her 4-year-old sister Opal to see Squatchy, their favorite band, pound out its brand of rock and punk.
Their mother drove them more than an hour from El Segundo and waited in the parking lot while the sisters watched the show.

An Arcadia restorer is reviving Bob Hope’s nativity set — and looking for its missing angel
By James Bartlett
Published November 21, 2026 at 5:00 AM PST
The nativity on display at Bob Hope’s estate in the 1980s.
Bob & Dolores Hope Foundation)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
Listen
4:05
Bob Hope's nativity display was the joy of Toluca Lake. One woman has been tapped to restore it
Josie Huang talks to writer James Bartlett.
Sheila Lehman got an unusual assignment in January to restore a nativity set owned by the late comedian Bob Hope.
Lehman, a seasoned craftsperson, owns and operates La Porte Vintage in Arcadia, which restores antique furniture and, more unusually, religious statues, most of them plaster.
Her specialty started about a dozen years ago, Lehman said, with her church, St. Bede in La Cañada Flintridge.
“One day the pastor came to me with a 100-year-old, 4-foot-tall wooden statue of Mary and Baby Jesus. It was in a very bad state — dry rot and more,” said Lehman, who’s established SaveLAStatues.org to bring awareness to the work she does.
The nativity set has 17 statues, including the shepherd, his son, Gaspar (one of the three kinds) and the bagpiper.
James Bartlett
LAist)
Since then, Lehman has restored several large-scale statues, like St. Agatha from St. Agatha’s Catholic Church on West Adams, and it’s become a larger part of her business. The Bob Hope nativity project is by far her biggest, and has taken most of the year. All that’s left to work on are now Mary, the cow and the camel.
Installation of the restored nativity is slated for the first week of December at the Plaza of the Cathedral of Our Lady of the Angels, in time for the Feast of Our Lady of Guadalupe on Dec. 12, a huge festival around the world, especially for Mexican and Mexican-American communities.
Sponsored message
Sheila Lehman is repairing a nativity set that belonged to Bob Hope.
James Bartlett
LAist)
A Toluca Lake Christmas tradition
Bob Hope — radio, television and movie star from the 1930s to the ‘90s — lived with his wife Dolores in Toluca Lake for decades. Neighbors still remember the Christmas treat of visiting the sprawling Hope estate to see the nativity.
Hope had purchased the hand-carved wooden set in the mid-1950s from an artisan company in Val Gardena in northern Italy, as a gift for Dolores, and every year Mary, Joseph, baby Jesus, the three kings, or Magi, and a selection of animals went on display, rain or shine.
Dolores carried the tradition on following her husband’s death at age 100 in 2003. After her death in 2011, the set — consisting of 17 statues measuring up to 5 feet. — was offered to their local parish, St. Charles Borromeo in North Hollywood.
It was then given to the Cathedral of Our Lady of the Angels in downtown Los Angeles, and went on display there from 2013 — again, outdoors.
The statue of Balthazar, before and after restoration.
Sheila Lehman)
Sponsored message
After some 70 years of being exposed to the elements, the figures were more than beginning to look their age.
“The donkey was really bad, but now he looks great. He has a very cute expression and posture. He might be my favorite,” Lehman said.
Rotted wood, faded paint and a moldy donkey
The cow statue being restored.
James Bartlett
LAist)
Lehman and her brother Kenny, who helps with cutting out rotted wood and replacing it with period-accurate linden wood, discovered that the set was likely a one-of-a-kind, custom order. Their research also included identifying the breed of cow, donkey and four sheep to ensure that they would be accurately repainted after repairing and sanding.
“We were really lucky, and got a call from the daughter of Adolph Fusek, who imported these sets from Europe. Jane remembered helping him do some repairs on this set years ago, and gave us some great advice,” Lehman said.
The same goes for the patterns and designs on the intricately flowing robes, none of which have been seen in their original glory for many decades.
Sponsored message
“The final painting is the part I love the most,” Lehman said, adding that there were some other surprises during the process, like the fluorescent yellow mold they found growing inside the donkey.
Camel attendant and St. Joseph statues.
James Bartlett
LAist)
“None of these statues should ever have been outside — it’s amazing that any of them survived at all,” she said.
Have you seen this angel?
Strangely, there is no angel in the nativity. It was never included in the collection when it was donated to the cathedral, and Sheila and her brother have so far failed to find a suitably sized replacement online.
“It’s definitely a mystery. Maybe someone has it in their yard or garage. Please get in touch if so! No questions asked,” she said.
After its December unveiling, the nativity will be up for Advent and Christmas, through Epiphany on Jan. 6.
Sponsored message
“It is going to be a little weird to give them back,” she said. “They've been here for so long, I feel responsible for them. I'm gonna be worrying about them.”

In coastal Orange County, a flood of anxiety ahead of November king tides
Jill Replogle
covers public corruption, debates over our voting system, culture war battles — and more.
Published November 20, 2026 at 5:50 PM PST
Sunset Beach, an enclave of Huntington Beach between the Pacific Ocean and Huntington Harbour, is preparing for major flooding during the ultra-high king tides expected over the Thanksgiving holiday.
Jill Replogle
LAist)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
A week before Thanksgiving, residents of Sunset Beach stacked sandbags, cleared garages and built makeshift barriers around their homes in a race against a gravitational clock. The year's highest ocean water levels, known as king tides, will arrive over the holiday, threatening this quaint coastal enclave of Huntington Beach with major flooding.
The king tides, which hit the California coast every year in November, December and January, are a normal phenomenon. They occur when the sun, moon and Earth align, combining their gravitational pull. But this year, the tides will be compounded by a prolonged marine heat wave, El Niño-fueled Kelvin waves and long-term sea level rise, which combined will likely add around 1½ feet to the predicted high tide, according to forecasters.
“We’re expecting the tides to be much higher than in October,” said Jessica Cuchilla, a spokesperson for the city of Huntington Beach. In late October, flooding during high tides damaged 114 homes in the harbor area, forcing some to move out. One home caught on fire when saltwater soaked a lithium-ion e-bike battery.
The Huntington Beach Fire Department made its own tide chart that accounts for the added sea level expected in this El Niño year.
Screenshot
LAist)
On the upside, Cuchilla said, “We’re much better prepared than we were in October.”
Read our guide to El Niño prepping
Now’s the time to get your family ready for El Niño. Here’s how to start
How one neighborhood is preparing
Bayview Drive on Sunset Island (part of Sunset Beach and also Huntington Harbour) was in full prepper mode on a recent morning. It was one of the hardest-hit areas during the high tides in late October. This time around, residents plan to be ready for the November arrival of the king tides.
Sponsored message
View this post on Instagram
Volunteers shoveled sand into bags, residents shuttled belongings out of their low-lying garages, and Tony Nobles, head of the Sunset Beach Community Association, strode down the street, making a mental checklist of work still needing to be done.
“ I think everybody here knows who I am now because I'm the one sending out all the emails,” he said before stopping to chat with a woman about plans for protecting her home and her elderly father’s home next door.  ”If you need anything, you know you can ask me, and I'll come,” Nobles told her.
Tony Nobles, head of the Sunset Beach Community Association, has been working around the clock to help fellow neighbors prepare for the king tides.
Jill Replogle
LAist)
Some of the homes on Sunset Island date back to the early 20th century, when the area was known for duck hunting in the adjacent marshes and as a landing spot for liquor smuggled in by boats during Prohibition. Each home is in charge of its own seawall or bulkhead to keep the harbor water at bay, and they are built to withstand a variety of sea-level heights. But ocean water that breaches a lower seawall can quickly become a problem for the whole neighborhood.
After the October high tides, the city of Huntington Beach sent code enforcement employees out to survey the entire harbor area, including Sunset Beach, totaling more than 3,000 homes. Workers posted notices ordering people to take measures to protect their property from flooding.
Preparing for El Niño
How to prepare your home for El Niño’s extreme weather
Now’s the time to take steps to protect your home from heavy rain, flooding and landslides that could come with this year’s potentially historic El Niño season.
With a strong El Niño expected in SoCal, should you consider flood insurance?
The weather pattern doesn’t guarantee flooding here, but now could be a good time to consider flood insurance, which is not included in most homeowners or renters policies.
SoCal drivers, get your car ready for El Niño's road hazards
El Niño’s signature heavy rains could make driving more risky than usual. Make sure your car is safe now, before extreme weather hits.
Sponsored message
Cuchilla, the city spokesperson, said most homeowners complied. The several dozen that didn’t, she said, were largely occupied by elderly or disabled residents who were unable to do the work themselves, she said. The city passed that list of homes to Nobles and Team Rubicon, a disaster response group, to help assess needs and deliver and stack sandbags.
View this post on Instagram
Huntington Beach is planning to shut down streets around the harbor during the upcoming king tides period, Nov. 23-27, to protect drivers, but also homeowners and businesses that can get flooded by the wakes left when vehicles plow through standing water. The city has also asked harbor residents to be ready to evacuate or shelter in place, if necessary.
What you need to know about El Niño
El Niño years can be associated with lots of rain in Southern California, though there's no guarantee of a deluge. And wet winters aren’t always disastrous. The man accused of sparking last year’s deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.
Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.
Rinderknecht, with little apparent reaction, gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. His father was present for the trial and as the verdict was read.
Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.
Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht’s first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial.
During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht’s state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. They did not focus as much on his resentment toward the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by “societal revenge” like they previously did.
Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire’s origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and cellphone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.
Sponsored message
They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.
“He was mad at everything, and frustrated,” said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams.
After the fire began, Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill. Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: “Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?”
These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.
They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked. Jurors were instructed not to consider the Los Angeles Fire Department’s role in putting out the fire.
Rinderknecht’s defense attorney Steve Haney casted doubt on the government’s case and said that their evidence proves nothing.
Haney said the fire scene could have been compromised because the area was accessible to the public until the Palisades Fire started Jan. 7.
Sponsored message
“Six days of anyone and everyone walking across the spot the government now calls a crime scene,” he said.
The defense called their own expert witnesses, including a retired fire investigator for the U.S. Forest Service who argued the fire origin area was different from what the government concluded.
Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing cell data records, and pointed to a neighbor’s testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trailhead.
He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht’s character, such as his angry text messages, because they were “evidence of the man, not evidence of the act.”
Finally, Haney presented an alternate explanation for what ignited the fire — fireworks. Multiple witnesses, including two neighbors and a local firefighter, all said they heard a loud bang or explosion from the direction of the hill the fire purportedly started on.
In the thousands of images of the evening collected from cameras in the area, none showed fireworks in the sky above the hill where the fire started, prosecutors said.

Even Orange County couldn’t escape the ‘bluenami’ this election season
By
Jill Replogle and
Destiny Torres
Published November 20, 2026 at 5:13 PM PST
O.C. Supervisor Katrina Foley, left, celebrates in Costa Mesa with supporter Susan Seely of Newport Beach as the first vote drop is announced during California's primary election on June 2, 2026.
Erin Stone
LAist)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
Orange County voters ensured a Democratic majority on the Board of Supervisors and gave the boot to three incumbent Republican state legislators in the 2026 election — a glaring sign of just how much demographics have changed in the once-red county and, local observers say, how much residents dislike the president.
“The outcome was way worse than we had anticipated,” said Will O’Neill, chairman of the Orange County Republican Party.
“The ‘bluenami’ … certainly didn't stop at the Pacific Ocean. We got swamped.”
What's left to count?
The Orange County Registrar of Voters announced Nov. 18 that all valid ballots had been counted. Still, there are still about 14,000 returned ballots that have not been counted, either because the voter didn’t sign the envelope or was a first-time voter who didn’t provide a government ID when registering.
The Registrar has notified those voters that they need to take extra steps to get their ballots counted, called “curing” (instructions are also available on the Registrar’s website), which voters need to complete by Nov. 25.
Final election results will be certified by December 11.
After the last general election in 2024, eight of the county’s 13 representatives in the state Assembly and Senate were Republicans. Come December, O.C. may send as few as four Republican representatives to Sacramento. (In one race, the Democratic candidate is ahead, but it’s still too close to call.)
Are these results evidence that this former bastion of the California GOP has abandoned the party? Not so fast, observers say. “ Orange County is still not Berkeley,” said Mike Moodian, a lecturer at Chapman University in Orange who specializes in local politics. “This isn't San Francisco. This isn't L.A. It's still a purple county, and there is still a strong Republican party in Orange County.”
“Purple” refers to a place with roughly equal portions of voters from different political parties. In O.C., Democrats make up 37% of registered voters, Republicans 33%, and voters who state No Party Preference or who belong to smaller parties make up 30%, according to data from the Orange County Registrar of Voters.
Sponsored message
O’Neill, the county GOP chair, pointed out that Republicans maintained, and in some cases gained, control over many city governments in the county. Those are technically nonpartisan races, meaning a candidate’s party does not appear next to their name on the ballot — a good thing for Republicans this year, he said.
“A lot of people just didn't want to vote for a Republican in this [election] cycle,” he said.
The reason for the party’s major losses this time around is simple, both O’Neill and Moodian said — President Donald Trump. But other observers cautioned against writing the election off to extreme dislike of the president.
“Clearly these are the demographics now,” said Tim Lineberger, an O.C.-based Republican political and PR consultant. Lineberger blamed the losses in part on the local GOP’s decision to divert resources to riskier races, away from ones he thinks they could have won. “You have to defend the places you can defend,” he said.
There are also indications that parts of the county where Democrats reliably win, in Santa Ana and surrounding cities, moved even further to the left in November.
Here’s a look at several key shifts that took place in the November election
Orange County Supervisor Katrina Foley won re-election in the November 2026 general.
Brian Feinzimer
LAist)
Sponsored message
A more progressive Board of Supervisors
A win in one of the two races on the ballot for the O.C. Board of Supervisors would have given Republicans a majority on the powerful board, which they last had in 2022, but the party came up short in both races.
In District 4, Democrat Connor Traut beat Republican Tim Shaw for the open seat by more than 8,000 votes. In District 5, incumbent Katrina Foley beat state Assemblymember Diane Dixon by close to 13,000 votes.
Along with Supervisor Vicente Sarmiento, who easily won re-election in the June primary, the new Democratic majority has a more progressive bent than the current one, where Democrat Doug Chaffee often votes with Republicans. Chaffee even endorsed Republican Dixon over Foley, his fellow Democrat and board colleague. What will that mean for the next term?
“I think we're going to see a Board of Supervisors that is aligned very well with labor,” Moodian said, noting that Traut and Foley were both heavily supported by labor unions in the election. Moodian said he’ll be watching how the new board approaches housing, homelessness, healthcare and plans for the LA28 Olympic and Paralympic Games, when O.C. will host several events.
Even fewer Republicans in Sacramento
Perhaps the most stunning Republican loss in O.C. was that of incumbent state Senator Tony Strickland in District 36, where Republicans have a five-percentage-point advantage in party registration over Democrats. Strickland, a Republican who lives in Huntington Beach, handily won a special election to fill the seat last year. He also beat out Democrat Chris Duncan in this year’s June primary, paving the way for a fall showdown.

Two proposed charter changes would roll back LA mayor's power
The changes would allow the Los Angeles City Council to override executive directives and remove general managers with a two-thirds vote.
Subscribe
Apple
Spotify
Topline:
The Los Angeles City Council on Friday referred to committee two proposed charter changes that would allow the council to overturn mayoral executive directives and remove department general managers, something only the mayor can do now. Any changes to the charter would require voter approval.
The details: Councilmember Monica Rodriguez authored the motion on executive directives, which are orders to department heads by the mayor. If approved, the council would need a two-thirds vote to override such an order. Rodriguez said the move was not aimed at incoming Mayor Nithya Raman, whom the council member did not support in the election. She said it's important that there be “healthy checks and balances ... regardless of who sits in the Mayor’s Office."
Councilmember Ysabel Jurado, who authored the motion on general managers, said it “grew out of serious concerns about the LAPD’s handling of protests” and the council’s “limited authority over department leadership.” As specified in the other motion, if approved, the City Council would need a two-thirds vote to remove a department manager.
Raman's reaction: Liz Garcia, a spokesperson for the mayor-elect, said Raman believes “eroding executive authority makes city government less efficient, less accountable and ultimately less effective in delivering services to residents."
What’s next: The City Council’s Ad Hoc Committee on Charter Reform plans to conduct a series of hearings on numerous proposed charter changes — including expanding the size of the council. It will be up to the full City Council to decide what changes to place before voters — likely on the November 2028 ballot.

LA used to have 14 toilets on sidewalks across the city, now it's down to four. What happened?
By Samhita Krishnan
Published November 20, 2026 at 2:52 PM PST
A standalone restroom run by the city of L.A. is one of four working sidewalk toilets in the Skid Row area.
Samhita Krishnan
LAist)
One year ago, Congress defunded public media. Now that we're 100% community funded, please become a sustaining member or increase your existing membership today.
The city of Los Angeles has a public bathroom problem.
Three years ago, LAist reported that in a city of nearly 4 million residents, there were only 14 permanent public toilets on the streets. Today, four of them work, according to city documents.
All four are on Skid Row.
The other 10, scattered from the San Fernando Valley to South L.A., are closed. Most shut down in July 2025, when the city’s 2025-26 budget included no money to operate them, according to the City Controller’s office.
Last month, Councilmembers Ysabel Jurado and Nithya Raman, now the city’s mayor-elect, introduced a motion calling on the city to fix the problem. It asks the city administrative officer to report within 60 days on a plan to keep the four Skid Row toilets funded and add more public toilets, handwashing stations and permanent water spigots across the city.
“This woefully inadequate scale of public hygiene infrastructure has left the streets of Los Angeles, especially in underinvested areas such as Skid Row, without consistent access to sanitation and water,” they wrote.
An interior view of a public restroom in downtown L.A.'s Skid Row.
Dana Littlefield
LAist)
Sponsored message
City sanitation crews collected more than 70 tons of human waste from the public right-of-way in 2025, according to the motion. LAist reached out to the city for information on how much waste was cleaned up in previous years, but did not get a response in time for publication.
Jurado’s office used more than $200,000 in discretionary funds to help keep the Skid Row toilets open.
“Our office committed discretionary funding and advocated during the budget process to keep four public restrooms open in Skid Row,” Jurado said in a statement. “But keeping essential facilities open cannot depend on individual council offices filling funding gaps year after year.”
How we got here
The four working toilets are the city’s standalone sidewalk toilets, run by the Bureau of Street Services, also known as StreetsLA. They are separate from restrooms inside city parks and libraries and from the app-operated Throne restrooms L.A. Metro has installed at more than 60 transit stations.
The city’s toilet shortage goes back decades. A 2001 deal with advertising company Outfront/JCDecaux could have put up to 150 self-cleaning toilets on city sidewalks, but permit delays left the city with just 14, LAist reported in 2023.
When that contract ended in 2022, the city replaced the toilets with its own, and StreetsLA said at the time that all 14 would be open by mid-April the following year.
Sponsored message
StreetsLA absorbed the cost of running all 14 toilets in fiscal year 2023-24, the Controller’s Office said, citing the bureau. The next year, the costs were covered largely by discretionary funds from Council District 14, which includes Skid Row. The 2025-26 budget left the program out.
This year, the City Council’s budget committee asked City Administrative Officer Matthew Szabo for ways to fund the toilets. StreetsLA estimated it would cost $1 million to operate the 10 closed toilets, but Szabo recommended against adding the money, according to a May budget memo the Controller’s office shared with LAist.
StreetsLA declined an interview request. In a statement, the bureau confirmed the four Skid Row toilets are open and said the city “is committed to identifying additional funding.”
It did not say when the others might reopen.
Inside the working bathrooms
According to the City Controller’s Office, the four open toilets are located at:
509 S. San Julian St.
814 E. 6th St.
204 E. 5th St.
545 S. San Pedro St.
On San Pedro Street near Sixth, the restroom is a squat cinder-block building painted with a mural of a blue heron in orange and green. Two sinks are set into its outside wall. The paint is chipped, peeling and tagged with graffiti, but the stalls inside were clean and stocked with toilet paper and soap.
Sponsored message
A worker from Five Keys Schools and Programs was stationed outside. The city has paid the nonprofit, which runs reentry programs for people leaving incarceration, to staff the Skid Row toilets since at least 2024, under a contract worth up to about $7.9 million a year that also covers mobile showers and Skid Row street cleaning.
A man working for the nonprofit Five Keys cleans the inside of a public restroom in L.A.'s Skid Row community.
Samhita Krishnan)
Under its Pit Stop program, attendants clean the stalls and nearby sidewalks, pick up used needles and hand out hygiene kits with soap, toothpaste and, for women, menstrual products, according to the nonprofit’s website. Five Keys says its Pit Stops serve about 50,000 visits a month at 15 sites downtown.
Richard Baker, who does community outreach for Five Keys and works at the Pit Stops in Skid Row, said the job goes beyond cleaning. He carries naloxone, also known by the brand name Narcan, a medication that can rapidly reverse an opioid overdose. And, he said, he helps people find food and shelter.
Richard Baker, who works with the nonprofit Five Keys, stands near one of the city's available public toilets in the Skid Row area.
Dana Littlefield
LAist)
